slot.brief: determine k so that a non-homogeneous 3×3 system has infinitely many solutions by enforcing Δ = 0 with a consistent numerator determinant

stem: If the system of equations $x + k y + z = 2$, $k x + y + z = -1$, $x + y + k z = -1$ has infinitely many solutions, then $k$ equals

verdicts.working: The coefficient determinant is $-(k-1)^2(k+2)$, so singularity requires $k=1$ or $k=-2$. At $k=1$, the equations have identical left sides but different right sides, so they are inconsistent. At $k=-2$, the right sides sum to zero, matching the dependence among the rows; the system is consistent and singular, hence has infinitely many solutions.

working:
Coefficient determinant: $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix}1 & k & 1\\ k & 1 & 1\\ 1 & 1 & k\end{vmatrix} = -(k-1)^2(k+2)$.

$\Delta = 0 \Rightarrow k = 1$ or $k = -2$.

For $k = 1$, the system becomes $x+y+z = 2,\; x+y+z = -1,\; x+y+z = -1$, which is inconsistent.

For $k = -2$, the equations are $x-2y+z = 2$, $-2x+y+z = -1$, $x+y-2z = -1$. Adding them gives $0 = 0$. The coefficient matrix has rank $2$ (e.g., the first two rows have minor $\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2\\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} = -3 \neq 0$) and the augmented matrix also has rank $2$ because the sum of the rows yields consistency. Hence infinitely many solutions exist only for $k = -2$.

Independent check: The coefficient determinant is $-(k-1)^2(k+2)$, so singularity requires $k=1$ or $k=-2$. At $k=1$, the equations have identical left sides but different right sides, so they are inconsistent. At $k=-2$, the right sides sum to zero, matching the dependence among the rows; the system is consistent and singular, hence has infinitely many solutions.
solution:
Infinitely many solutions require the coefficient determinant to vanish:
$$\Delta=-(k-1)^2(k+2)=0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad k=1\text{ or }-2.$$
For $k=1$, the equations are inconsistent. For $k=-2$, their sum is $0=0$, and the coefficient matrix has rank $2<3$, so the system has infinitely many solutions. Hence $k=-2$.
